hints: Focus on what happens to excess fertiliser when it rains, does it stay put in the field or move with water?
Remember the solubility rule for ammonium salts and nitrates, both ions form compounds that are very soluble and do not precipitate.
Link that highly soluble, mobile nitrate ion to where groundwater goes next and why nitrate in drinking water is a health concern.
walkthrough:
**See what NH4NO3 does in water**

Think like water for a moment. Ammonium nitrate is an ionic fertiliser that dissolves completely and easily.

$$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3(s) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{NO}_3^-(aq)$$
This means excess fertiliser does not sit as a solid. It forms mobile ions.

**Follow those ions when it rains**

Plants can only take up so much nitrogen. The rest is washed down through the soil by rain, a process called leaching.

Because all nitrates are soluble, $\text{NO}_3^-$ stays dissolved and travels into groundwater and rivers instead of forming a precipitate.

**Spot the real environmental problem**

Nitrate-rich groundwater may later be abstracted for drinking water. High nitrate in drinking water is a health risk and also causes eutrophication in rivers and lakes.

That matches the idea of soluble fertiliser reaching groundwater used for drinking.

options.A: Incorrect. Excess $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ does not make soil alkaline. If anything, ammonium-based fertilisers tend to make soil more acidic over time due to nitrification which releases $\text{H}^+$. Students choosing this confuse ammonium with a base.
options.B: Incorrect. Rain does wash $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ into rivers, but it does not form a precipitate there. All ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble, so $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ stay in solution and cause eutrophication, not precipitation.
options.C: Correct. $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ is very soluble, so excess leaches through soil into groundwater as dissolved $\text{NH}_4^+$ and especially $\text{NO}_3^-$. If that groundwater is used for drinking, high nitrate is a recognised health and environmental problem.
options.D: Incorrect. This mixes up acid-base ideas. Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) is basic, so if it formed it would raise pH, not lower it. In reality, soil acidity from these fertilisers comes from oxidation of $\text{NH}_4^+$ to nitrate releasing $\text{H}^+$, not from ammonia lowering pH.
